utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, distinguished Judges of the trial, as in our initial presentation, I will set fourth our overall case and Mr. Kehoe and Mr. Misetic will elaborate on the evidence. It is our submission in rebuttal that the Prosecution pleadings on this motion are wholly unresponsive to the substance of our pleadings. If anything, those submissions confirm our suspicion throughout these proceedings that the entire case against General Gotovina has been based on fundamentally flawed assumptions as to the applicable legal standards. The Prosecution treats the catch-all count of persecution as a black hole in which humanitarian law disappears. In particular, the Prosecution treats its core theory of unlawful attacks under Count 1 as an abstract accusation that if repeated enough times, somehow dispenses with the requirement to prove any particular violation of the laws of war. Similarly, the Prosecution treats JCE as a concept that is so elastic that it can be stretched in every possible direction; a kind of well-cooked legal soup where the requirement of distinct legal ingredients is blurred into an indistinguishable whole. Mr. Russo's pleading on Count 1 makes much of the view that when charged as an element of persecution, unlawful attacks may be isolated but widespread and systematic in conjunction with other crimes. Mr. Russo further asserts at page 17392, lines 3 to 5, and I quote: "That the Gotovina Defence has incorrectly argued that the unlawful attack is at the core of the Prosecution's case theory against General Gotovina." Mr. Russo wholly disregards the Prosecution's repeated case that "the shelling of Knin and other towns was at the core of the plan to drive Serbs out." And that is once again a quote from Mr. Tieger's opening statement at page 443, lines 24 to 25. Are we now being told that if the Prosecution could prove a few isolated cases of unlawful shelling, which we submit it cannot, that such proof could sustain a conviction for a JCE alleging mass terrorisation and mass expulsion under Article 5? The Prosecutor's pre-trial brief states clearly at paragraph 11 that after Operation Storm, all but a small fraction of the civilian population had left. Mr. Tieger's opening statement states that very few civilians were left after Krajina's liberation. This is at page 418, line 14. So if there is no evidence of large-scale unlawful shelling, how could burning and looting be the basis for mass expulsion when everybody left before any Croatian soldiers arrived? The Prosecution JCE theory of mass expulsion can only stand if there is proof of widespread or systematic attacks in violation of the laws of war. But the best is yet to come, in Mr. Russo's pleading. He submitted not only that isolated incidents of unlawful shelling are legally sufficient to prove the Prosecution case, but that, additionally, there is not even a requirement of proving civilian death or injury or destruction resulting from such attacks. This is at page 17391, lines 9 to 25. We were referred to the Kordic Appeals judgement, paragraph 105, in support of this proposition. And, indeed, Mr. Russo is correct that the Appeals Chamber in that case does not require results, such as death or injury to civilians. But if we read the case carefully, and we go to the Kordic trial judgement at paragraph 204, it becomes apparent that the Appeals judgement is referring to the persecutory act of attack or bombardment by whatever means of undefended towns, villages, dwellings, or buildings, a violation of the laws or customs of war enumerated under Article 3(C) of the Statute. This provision corresponds to Article 59 of Protocol I which is based on Article 25 of the 1907 Hague regulations on land warfare. An attack against an undefended town does not require proof of death or injury, because it is unlawful as such. Since there are no military objectives whatsoever in an undefended town, there is no need for further inquiry. But that is not the case before this Chamber. The Prosecution has not charged this prohibited act anywhere in the indictment. On the contrary, during the testimony of Kosta Novakovic, the Prosecution stipulated on the record that they were not claiming that Knin was ever an open city, and expressly waived the argument that it was undefended. This is at page 11909, line 1, to page 11911, line 17. It is astonishing that we are now presented for the first time with the argument that attacks on Knin and other locations were unlawful as such because they were supposedly undefended. This is a flagrant instance of the Prosecution playing fast and loose with humanitarian law, of treating persecution as a charge in which the specific actus reus can be arbitrarily changed even after the conclusion of the case in chief. The Prosecution cannot now plead a new substantive charge of attacks against undefended towns under Article 59 of Protocol I. It has only charged in the indictment unlawful attacks against civilians and civilian objects, and it has only referred to Article 59(2) [sic] at trial. Furthermore, based on Article 59(2) of Protocol I, the Prosecution's unlawful shelling case would be dead upon arrival. The Prosecution would have to prove that Knin and other locations behind ARSK front lines were open for occupation by an adverse party, as stipulated under Article 59(2). Based on the facts, such a case is manifestly absurd. If I may, just for the sake of the transcript, indicate that at line 10 -- on page 10, line 3, the reference to Article 59(2) should be Article 51(2). Thank you. The Prosecution thus cannot avoid the requirement of unlawful attacks under Article 51(2) to prove to once again cite the Galic trial judgement at paragraph 56, that in addition the mens rea of willfully making civilians the object of acts of violence, that those acts must in fact have caused death or serious injury to body or health within the civilian population. The fact that Galic was decided after Kordic should leave no doubt that the Judgement distinguished between Article 51 and 59 of Protocol I in requiring results such as civilian death or injury. As Mr. Kehoe will explain, the Prosecution case taken at its highest is that there was shelling in different parts of Knin. Beyond speculation, based on observation at some distance, there is not a single instance where an unlawful attack is conclusively proven. To the contrary, the UNMO report, to give just one example, that's Exhibit P64, concludes that artillery fire was concentrated in the close vicinity of military objectives and caused minimal damage. What is most significant for these proceedings, however, is that there is no proof whatsoever of a single civilian death or injury resulting from an unlawful attack. Mr. Russo has, for the first time, referred to 50 to 75 deaths allegedly resulting from unlawful attacks. This is at page 17402, lines 7 to 10. We would be grateful if the Prosecution could identify these alleged victims and what evidence is now being adduced to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that they in fact were not combatants or if they were civilians, that they were victims of unlawful attacks rather than incidental casualties of lawful combat operations. The Prosecution provides no specific evidence because it has none. In this regard, we note the Blaskic Appeals judgement at paragraph 114, ruling that with respect to charges of unlawful attack, and I quote: "The specific situation of the victim at the time the crimes are committed may not be determinative of his civilian or non-civilian status. If he is indeed a member of an armed organisation, the fact that he is not armed or in combat at the time of the commission of the crimes, does not accord him civilian status." If, as Mr. Tieger dramatically note, thousands of shells were raining upon civilians, why has the Prosecution not succeeded, after 14 years, to prove a single civilian death or injury, or damage to civilian objects resulting from an unlawful attack? It is telling that Mr. Russo's main argument that the use of MBRLs constituted an indiscriminate attack was actually based on Prosecution witness Rajcic's testimony, that this weapon was in fact not used against Milan Martic's headquarters because it was considered to be insufficiently accurate for that specific military objective in an urban context. This is at page 17400, lines 4 to 7. Instead of drawing the only reasonable inference that Croatian forces did not use MBRLs in an indiscriminate fashion, Mr. Russo instead concludes that they did because, and I quote from page 17401, lines 20 to 21, that: "Kari Anttila testified that he conducted a crater analysis of six MBRL impacts in that same residential area and that buildings and cars were damaged." Perhaps Mr. Russo has forgotten Judge Orie's question to Mr. Anttila, at pages 2687 to 2688, demonstrating that the MBRLs were in fact fired by the ARSK from Strmica. So the Prosecution's only crater analysis in this casei n support of its mass terror JCE is based on a single crater analysis with respect to MBRLs that were in fact fired by the other party to the conflict. In view of the applicable law, the Prosecution core theory of unlawful shelling manifestly fails whatever imaginative last minute theory or distortions of facts are now set forth. The Trial Chamber may recall that Judge Orie specifically asked the Prosecution's star witness Ambassador Galbraith at page 5055, lines 21 to 23: "Did you consider the purpose of Operation Storm primarily to expel the Serbs?" His clear answer was: "No, not at all." When Judge Orie sought clarification, Ambassador Galbraith stated categorically at page 5057, lines 7 to 8: "I do not think Operation Storm was taken for the purpose of expelling the Serbs from Croatia." That is the Prosecution's star witness. We cannot help asking ourselves whether the Prosecution ever did a proper assessment of the evidence before indicting General Gotovina. In dismissing this JCE theory, the Trial Chamber need only consider other unlawful shelling cases, in Galic, Blaskic, Kordic, Strugar, Martic, to conclude that a conviction cannot be sustained under Count 1. Indeed, we would respectfully submit that this is the most untenable weakest ever unlawful shelling case in the history of this Tribunal. Consequently, its dismissal would be entirely appropriate and consistent with a fair and expeditious trial. As set forth in our prior pleadings, there can be no case of mass deportation through unlawful shelling if in fact there is no proof of unlawful shelling. This is a matter of elementary logic and one needs only to look at the Prosecution's consistent theory to conclude that a conviction on Count 1 in relevant part and Counts 2 and 3 in whole, depends entirely on proof of causation between unlawful attacks and forced displacement. How else could such displacement, which is in fact pursuant to RSK evacuation orders, how else could it be on grounds not permitted in international law, as required by Articles 5(d) and (i). What other factual basis is there to establish a widespread or systematic deportation if, as the Prosecution has repeatedly admitted, there were very few civilians remaining in Krajina once the Croatian soldiers actually arrived. It is also remarkable that the Prosecution persists in its argument that there is no requirement of control over territory with respect to deportation and forcible transfer. Article 49 of the 4th Geneva Convention stipulates in relevant part that: "Individual or mass forcible transfers, as well as deportations of protected persons from occupied territory ... are prohibited." But the Prosecution contends that there is no such requirement when it is charged under Article 5, such that it applies to displacement as a result of shelling prior to occupation. The Prosecution has completely ignored the authorities we have cited in this motion. It relies on the Stakic Appeals judgement to argue that Article 49 of the 4th Geneva Convention does not apply to the actus reus of Articles 5(d) or (i). But paragraph 306 of the Stakic Appeals judgement states categorically that Article 49 is "the underlying instrument prohibiting deportation." In the Krnojelac Appeals judgement, Judge Schomburg's separate opinion confirms at paragraph 13 that deportation under Article 5 requires: "The removal of someone from the territory over which the person removing others exercises sovereign authority." This language is identical with Stakic Trial judgement at paragraph 674 and is consistent with the Krnojelac trial judgement at paragraph 473, both of which we have previously cited. We also refer to Judge Schomburg's separate and partly dissenting opinion in the Naletilic Appeals judgement which is not dissenting on this particular issue at paragraph 22. The Prosecution's persistence on this untenable theory of deportation only reinforces the view that these charges should have never been made in the first place, as we argued in our Rule 72 pre-trial submissions. In relation to discriminatory intention for Count 1, we note that there is some confusion as to whether President Tudjman or General Gotovina is on trial in this case. The obsessive focus on President Tudjman's view of multi-ethnic states is hardly a basis for proving that dolus specialis on the part of General Gotovina with respect to a crime that is but one step away from genocide, to quote, once again the Kupreskic trial judgement. Mr. Tieger argues that members of the Croatian political and military leadership, including the accused had a discriminatory intent, but then proceeds to quote only from two speeches of President Tudjman. This is at page 17389, line 1, to 17390, line 21. It is also difficult to understand how Mr. Waespi concludes that General Gotovina's orders to guard Serbian Orthodox churches to prevent their destruction is in fact proof of his discriminatory intent to allow burning and looting of Serbian property. This is at page 17429, line 18, to page 17430, line 7. The Prosecution seems to believe that merely because the Croatian RSK conflict was defined on ethnic lines, any military commander participating in combat is presumed to be acting with discriminatory intention. For this reason alone, Count 1 should be dismissed. In relation to the remainder of the case, that is, whether beyond unlawful shelling, burning and looting was part of the Brioni JCE, Mr. Tieger once again admitted the Prosecution's disregard for the applicable law. He simply argued at page 17385, line 25, to page 1738 [sic], line 2, that there was no need to specify every means for implementing the removal of Serbs and certainly not those particular means. He goes on to insist that there is no basis in common sense for such a requirement. Whatever Mr. Tieger's perception may be of common sense, proof of particular crimes is in fact a requirement of the law of JCE. Ever since the Tadic Appeals judgement, the settled law has clearly required proof of intention in relation to particular crimes. With respect to JCE category 1, Tadic held at paragraph 196 that: "All co-defendants acting pursuant to a common design possess the same criminal intention. For instance, the formulation of a plan among the co-perpetrators to kill where in effecting this common design, they all possess the intent to kill." This authority was most recently confirmed in the Krajisnik trial judgement and upheld by the Appeals judgement at paragraph 200 to the effect that the JCE participants must have, to quote, "a common state of mind that the statutory crimes forming part of the objective should be carried out." Mr. Tieger's admission confirms once again that throughout this trial the Prosecution case has been based upon the flawed legal theory that a broad and vague Brioni JCE aimed at alleged removal of Serbs does not require proof of a shared intention to commit specific crimes under the Statute. This renders JCE so elastic that a mere allegation of persecution would encompass everything from extermination to discriminatory denial of employment. There is simply no proof that there was an agreement in Brioni to commit plunder and destruction. There is also no proof that General Gotovina ever made a significant contribution to such crimes, which he in fact actively opposed, or that he otherwise ordered, instigated or aided and abetted their commission. Finally, with respect to Article 7(3) liability, we note first in relation to liability for murder and cruel treatment that the Oric Appeals judgement, at paragraphs 58 to 59, specifically held that knowledge of the crime and knowledge of the subordinate's criminal conduct are not one and the same, even within the confines of a prison, as contrasted to the large territory implicated in the present case. The Prosecution has offered no evidence whatsoever that General Gotovina had any notice that his subordinates in particular were responsible for murder or cruel treatment. We note further that in her submissions, Ms. Gustafson did not respond at all to the Halilovic Appeals judgement, indicating that rights of intervention over the military police cannot be the basis for attribution of command responsibility to General Gotovina when there is no additional evidence that criminal investigations were in fact within his competence or material ability to act. Once again, these are issue that the Prosecution should have carefully considered at the indictment phase, let alone at this stage of the trial. Finally, Mr. President, I will briefly address your questions concerning the partial dismissal of counts under Rule 98 bis. Our submission is that the evidence cannot sustain a conviction on any of the counts and we therefore respectfully request the Chamber to enter a judgement of acquittal on all counts. In the alternative, it is our submission that the Chamber has the discretion under Rule 98 bis to dismiss counts in part. Judicial opinion in this regard not uniform. However, our position is consistent with that of the Trial Chamber in Oric in discussing the object and purpose of the amended Rule 98 bis. At page 7857, line 24, to 785, line 3, of the transcript of the Oric trial, the Court says as follows: "We have opted for 'count' rather than 'offences charged' or 'charges' with the understanding that everyone will try to understand that behind the purpose of Rule 98 bis, there is not ... a humongous exercise to be undertaken to deal with the minutiae of the events mentioned during the testimony." Further on at page 7858, line 19, to 7859, line 10, the Trial Chamber goes on to say: "We will, of course, be prepared to hear evidence if there is a submission that, for example, in regard to a particular person mentioned in the indictment that's supposed to have been the victim of cruel treatment or the victim of murder, it's the submission of the Defence that there was absolutely no evidence at all adduced by the Prosecution or that the evidence adduced is -- can [sic] sustain a conviction. Then I think - and we have discussed this amongst ourselves - we will entertain submissions, short submissions, on that score because ultimately it will be in the benefit of the economy of justice that the defence is put on notice that ... as far as regards the alleged murder of -- there is absolutely no way that the Trial Chamber can ultimately come to a conviction so that they don't have to lose or waste time in trying to bring forward evidence in that regard, even though they have no burden of proof, but particularly because they have a right to remain silent. So that right ought to be -- ought to be respected." In the alternative, if this Trial Chamber does not concur with the views in Oric, we submit that the earlier version of Rule 98 bis be applied pursuant to Rule 6(D). The indictment was confirmed in 2001. The case has been pending since then, and the failure to dismiss counts in part clearly prejudices the rights of the defendant to a fair and expeditious trial, and accordingly, we request relief in this regard, should that be necessary. Finally, Mr. President, we note in addition to our arguments on the scope of Rule 98 bis, that it is within the inherent powers of this Trial Chamber, in the interests of a fair and expeditious trial, to make such findings as it considers appropriate to indicate whether it considers evidence in relation to part of counts, to be irrelevant or unnecessary in view of its appreciation of the Prosecution case in chief thus far. We refer in particular to unlawful attacks as a persecutory count -- persecutory act under Count 1 and the inextricable allegations of deportation and forcible transfer arising from unlawful shelling under Counts 1 to 3. We also refer to a significant number of the scheduled killings that the Prosecution has refused to drop. So, in conclusion, we submit that there is no reason in principle why the Trial Chamber could not avoid significant costs and delays in this trial by indicating specific offences where it is unnecessary for the defendant to answer the Prosecution case. Whether this is achieved through a Rule 98 bis or any other ruling that the Chamber considers appropriate, the underlying objective, we submit, should be the fair and expeditious conduct of the remainder of this trial, especially when there are serious flaws in the core theory of the Prosecution case in chief. Before concluding, Mr. President, I also want to note that in the transcript at page 18, line 15, this is an error and it should read never sustain a conviction. Just to correct the record. I thank you for your patience and kind attention. I now request the Chamber to ask -- my colleague Mr. Kehoe to continue our pleadings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. President, if I may proceed with the Chamber's permission. I would like to back and cover some of the topics that were not covered by the Office of the Prosecutor in their rather interesting argument yesterday where, for the first time, we are to infer and not -- a variety of facts and circumstances in light of other facts which, frankly, the Office of the Prosecutor chose to ignore. Once again the centrepiece of their argument with -- concerning this JCE and also with regard to the alleged unlawful shelling of Knin is Brioni. And once again they fail or refuse, and I suspect it's the latter, to contextualise exactly that meeting says and where it fits into the chronology of events. What we know prior to 31st of July of 1995, as does the Prosecutor know, that a directive -- that there was even before that, there was planning for the retaking of Knin with grid references and targeting done as far back as 1993. What we know, moving closer to Operation Storm, that on the 26th of June, 1995, the HV Main Staff gave instructions to the Military Districts to plan Operation Storm using artillery and using rockets to be fired upon military objectives in Knin and Benkovac, a month prior to Brioni. What do we know after Brioni? We know that on the 1st of August of 1995 that Ambassador Galbraith came to see President Tudjman to discuss the retaking -- the military retaking of Knin where he cautioned that the HV had to respect the rights of civilians. We know that on that same date General Gotovina ordered his officers, that Operation Storm was to achieve a military victory, and that they were -- it was to be aimed only against enemy soldiers. The one big thing that we also know that came post-Brioni that wasn't discussed by the Prosecutor are two very important events. Number one, they had less ammunition to fire. If you look at the order from the HV Main Staff from the 26th of June, D956, where they ordered that they would have six sets for the artillery, the Kozjak order of the 2nd of August, because of limited -- limited ammunition ordered only four. So in this -- in addition to that, in addition to less ammunition, this alleged attack on the civilian population with this less ammunition also brought with it a firing on a town that wasn't even in Knin. That town being Drvar. Drvar being a town that was being held by the Bosnian Serbs in the Republic of Srpska. Again, not described by Mr. Russo, that is one of the towns, along with Knin, Obrovac, Gracac, and Benkovac, that was to be fired upon. So if we are to take the theory as presented by the Prosecution, where this -- General Gotovina ordered the indiscriminate fire on these towns, to drive the Krajina Serb population out, we have indiscriminate fire on a town in Bosnia-Herzegovina where there was no Krajina Serbs -- or were no Krajina Serbs. It's an interesting argument to ponder. And let us assume for the sake of argument that the shelling was to drive the Serb -- the Krajina Serbs out of the Krajina. What we know, Mr. President, Your Honours, is that the HV never fired on Knin prior to the 4th of August of 1995. And I cite you to Marko Rajcic in the trial transcript, page 16619, line 1, through 16620, line 4. And if this was anything akin to the situation in Sarajevo, Mr. President, I'm sure that the Chamber would have heard any amount of evidence on that score which it did not. And we also know that after the retaking of Grahovo the HV was in position or in excellent position to do just that, fire upon Knin and they did not. How about the issue that they forced the Krajina Serbs to leave. Well, once again the Prosecutor overlooked what was well known to the internationals, as was reflected in Ambassador Galbraith's diary for June 15th of 1995, that is set forth in P458, which was that if the HV came to retake the Krajina that the Serbs would leave. The Prosecution called Marko Rajcic, the author of the artillery section of the Kozjak order, as well as the attack order for artillery that was an attachment thereto. He explained to the Chamber exactly what the language meant and what was understood by the language set forth in that order which was the following: Attack military installations and that they were to be guided by the principles of distinction and proportionality. The fact of the matter is, one again that is not discussed, in this endeavour to drive the -- alleged drive the Krajina Serb population out of the Krajina, the vast majority of artillery and rocket fire was against front line positions being held by the ARSK and not on the towns set forth in the order. What is -- things are quite clear, that the target selection had been made prior to Brioni, that civilians, per Marko Rajcic, were not to be targeted, and in fact they attempted to minimise civilian casualties and damage to civilian property. I cite Your Honours to D1425, paragraph 17. Let us next look at the allegations of the Prosecutor concerning the weaponry that was used. Mr. Russo said at page 17399, line 25, over to the following page: "General Gotovina choose to use unguided multi-barrel rocket-launcher systems, an unquestionably indiscriminate weapon under the circumstances." There is absolutely no evidence in the record to substantiate that position. To the contrary. Again, the Prosecutor overlooked the statement of the Prosecutor's expert Colonel Konings, who noted at page 14758, lines 11 to 15, that multi-barrel rocket launchers could be directed against military targets. Likewise, Marko Rajcic noted that the weapon systems that they chose, the T-130s and the 122 MRLs, were capable of being directed and hitting military objectives and that they were used in that fashion. Suffice it to say, what is also lacking in the case presented by the Prosecution is the whole idea of any type of disproportionate damage. Has there been one scintilla of evidence presented to this Chamber that would lead the Chamber or could lead the Chamber to conclude that there was some type of disproportionate damage that was brought to bear against the civilian population because of a weapon system that had been employed? The answer to that question is no. Merely finding a rocket or a piece of artillery in a civilian neighbourhood does not render the -- does not lead to a disproportionality argument as set forth by the Prosecution. With regard to the arguments as set forth again by Mr. Russo at 17394 of the transcript at line 10 to 134, where he maintains that the shelling was not done to knock out the command and control of the ARSK but rather -- I want to quote him as accurately as possible, but was in fact directed at the civilian population. What's interesting to note is that he overlooks the fact that as a result of the shelling, communications were in fact destroyed, as we know from Witness 56, which led to the line being breached up in the Dinara being held by those troops under Witness 56's command, as reflected in General Mrksic's interview with the BBC, which is D1258, and also in General Mrksic's report, D923, page 6, where he highlights the -- or describes the defeat of the ARSK coming from the breach in the lines by the HV being held by Witness 56's troops. Next, the issue concerning panic. One issue that Mr. Russo emphasised on 173 -- 17399. Lieutenant -- he notes on line 4, Lieutenant Konings testified that this type of prolonged shelling with single rounds would have almost no effect on the military itself. Of course, counsel did not read the cross-examination of Colonel Konings where he noted in line -- on page 14538, in response to my questioning at line 12: "Well, under the circumstances and the information you were given, harassing fire going into Knin can be used against the military to cause confusion, suppress movement and lower morale. Isn't that right? "Answer: Yes." And we can see the actual impact on the ARSK military of the shelling in P1256, D1257, and very interestingly the shelling going into the northern barracks in D930, at Mr. Vrcalj's book, where no one would even go out and assist him to travel downtown because they were afraid for their lives. Lastly, Mr. Russo's line on page 31394, that there was no plan to defend. As a rationale for him arguing that the shelling was unnecessary, he noted there was no plan to defend the town from in [sic]. Again, we can look at General Mrksic's report which shows quite the contrary, D923, at page 3; General Mrksic's interview with Radio Belgrade on the night of the 4th where he is talking about engaging in the direct defence of Knin, D106; and which is likewise supported against by another Prosecution -- Captain Dangerfield at P693, which noted that the Krajina Serbs were headed for a bloody last stand in Knin. In an effort to show that the attack was indiscriminate, Mr. Russo presented the -- a chart to Your Honours with a -- numerous circles on there, most of which came from Mr. Dreyer. I mean, one of them, for instance, was from Mira Grubor who never saw any artillery until the 5th. And I would point Your Honours to the questioning by the Chamber of Mr. Dreyer when the Chamber saw this exhibit with most of these circles on it. And I cite the Chamber to page 10855, line 2, through page 856, line 12. And if I can paraphrase the colloquy, and it was with you Judge Orie and the witness, the questioning was -- you were asking questions concerning what the witness saw and he noted that the -- when he saw the shelling, he noted that the areas around the military objectives incurred the most intense bombardment and that he had witnessed a few impacts at areas where there were no military objectives. So clearly what he was saying and, of course, the Chamber has the record before it, that the fire was concentrated on military targets. Quite similar to the conclusion that was made by Steiner Hjertnes, a witness not called by the Prosecution, whose report is reflected in P64. And we also know based on Mr. Roberts, that he came up to a similar conclusion in his final report. The conclusions of Mr. Hjertnes, of course, were consistent with those found by, as we see in D66, a US cable that was sent shortly after Operation Storm, 14 August 1995, which notes: "Although Knin was reportedly heavily shelled in the early hours of hostilities, few buildings and residential areas showed signs of shell damage." This is consistent again with another HV -- OTP witness Mr. Flynn who went on the 7th of August, 1995, and he noted on 1302 that he was surprised at the lack of shelling. With the little time I have left I would like to address the killings issue that has come to bear because in fact Mr. Russo, in his submission at page 17402, noted that 50 to 57 civilians were killed as a result of the shelling and 30 to 40 more injured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One thousand. It was early on in the trial, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, I was with totally different witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise. Yes, I may have misspoken in the speed.

utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may just say this, Judge, what we have before us is -- are 37 victims in a joinder indictment and now 337 alleged victims in a further clarification schedule. At this juncture in the trial, it is incumbent upon the Prosecution if they maintain, as Mr. Russo did yesterday, that 50 to 75 civilians were killed in this unlawful attack, this shelling, to name them. To name this 50 to 75 people in this clarification schedule and to do so tomorrow. We -- the Defence is entitled to such notice and is required for a fair trial for the Defence to be able to meet this. Lastly, and my last point is with regard to cluster munitions by Mr. Dawes. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Two points. One is that we were told by Mr. Registrar that we began at 2.48 and I believe you'd indicated that --

utterances.text: That's great. Then please proceed. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to quibble over a few minutes for the Defence, however, the exchanging of time, I think, is inappropriate. The Prosecution is -- was pressed for time, perhaps everyone is, I accept that. But I don't think that -- those were the ground rules before and I don't think -- as I say, if in terms of these few minutes, I trust that -- that's not the standard of the practice here and I don't intend to make a fuss about that. But to change the ground rules entirely, I think it is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, you may have heard Mr. Tieger object as a matter of principle but at the same time doesn't want to spend a lot of time on the few minutes that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. And we object as a matter of principle to the fact that, as it turned out, the Prosecution spent three hours with respect to General Gotovina and a half an hour apiece with respect to Generals Cermak and Markac which is what results, of course, in the fact that we've worked out amongst ourselves how to deal with the four-hour presentation that the Prosecution did yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Views of both parties in this respect are clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, Your Honours, you will recall that a little over a year ago in the opening statements the Defence of General Gotovina told you that you would be asked by the Defence to take the simple straightforward view of the evidence and that you would be asked by the Prosecution at the end of the day to take the complicated conspiracy theories and to twist the facts in order to fit a particular conspiracy theory. As it turns out, over a year later, yesterday you heard such things from the Prosecution as General Gotovina's defence of Serb Orthodox churches should be held against him. You heard such things as the necessary and reasonable measure was to keep criminal elements in the army, and that to let criminal elements out of the army was a reckless thing to do. You didn't hear the Prosecution address any of the evidence that overwhelmingly contradicts their theory of the case. And we submit, Your Honours, that in light of the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, that is a fatal flaw in their case and also reveals the fact that their inability to deal with the hard evidence in the case reveals the fact, as I said, that you have to accept the complicated conspiracy theory and ignore the straightforward evidence. The way they suggest this, of course, is through the use of the word "inference." You are to draw inferences from certain evidence that they put forward. We call your attention to the Blaskic Appeals judgement of 29 July 2004, where the Appeals Chamber found that the Trial Chamber erred when it drew inferences which were inconsistent with the evidence in the trial record. This is at paragraph 520 through 525, particularly paragraph 522. What didn't they address yesterday? And after all, this is a 98 bis motion and not final argument and therefore I will focus on what wasn't discussed. What they didn't dispute was that General Lausic was in command and control of the military police in its crime investigation, crime prevention and crime prosecution function. What they didn't dispute is that no matter theory they come up with on mens rea for murder, no witness was able to substantiate their theory and Mr. Theunens, again, an in-house OTP witness put forward as an expert, was unable or unwilling to go along with the OTP's view of sanitation documents. They completely ignore in their JCE context, all of the orders issued before Operation Storm, both oral and written, whether by Minister Susak or General Gotovina, the military or the civil police. Completely ignored in their presentation yesterday. Why? Because they can't deal with it. And we submit under the Blaskic Appeals judgement that per se precludes you from draw drawing negative inferences when there's specific evidence in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, you are --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm aware. I have -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you have the disadvantage of not having someone who holds you at a lower speed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The Prosecution states an incorrect or at least incomplete standard with respect to mens rea. The standard is not simply whether General Gotovina was notified of the risk of such offences. The Blaskic Appeals Chamber makes clear that such a standard would amount to a negligent standard. The standard is not whether the accused has knowledge of the mere possibility of crimes but, rather, that there is a substantial likelihood that crimes will be committed. Furthermore, in the interests of time, I call the Chamber's attention to paragraphs 344 through 348 of the Blaskic Appeals decision which dismissed very similar arguments to the ones advanced by the Prosecution here attempting to ascribe mens rea to General Gotovina for murder. With respect to Mr. Hedaraly's presentation, first the Prosecution files a first clarification. Then in July 2008 they advise Chamber that after having conducted a comprehensive review of the body of material on its exhibit list, they need to withdraw 59 names. But they add 189. Then after the comprehensive review is conducted, nevertheless, yesterday they're required to withdraw another 32. Mr. Hedaraly's explanation for this is that yes, some of those victims have no autopsy reports, have no name, et cetera, but then the best example he can put forward is, beginning at page 17417, the case of Ilija Mirkovic, Mr. Hedaraly says testified the Croatian soldiers entered the hamlet on 5 August, this is the hamlet of Zagrovic. And then Mr. Hedaraly says then he discovered Jovo Dmitrovic's body, who is victim 129. However, if you look at the further clarification, victim 129 is alleged to have been killed on the 16th of August. So the first inference to be drawn is that the HV entered the village on the 5th of August, which means that a person killed on the 16th of -- on the 5th of August, I should say, which means that someone killed on the 16th must have been killed by the HV. Building from there, Mr. Hedaraly says 12 victims died in the same village of Zagrovic "shortly after the end of military operations," and suggests that these 12 individuals must have been killed by the HV that entered the village on the 5th of August. But if you look at the further clarification, in some of these it is actually 15 -- the dates of death range from 5 August, some to 9 August, two on 16 August, one on 1 September, 25 August, 18 September, and 20 September. Mr. President, it stretches credulity that the Prosecution's theory of murder for many of these individuals without any other corroborating evidence is that the HV entered a village on the 5th and therefore if someone was killed on the 16th or later, that must be ascribed to the HV. Why do I bring this up? Because the standard apparently for the Prosecution is that we should take their word for it. There's no evidence in the record to support this. The Prosecution acknowledges in their argument that for many of these it all depends on the Prosecution's oral representations but we should take their word for it. More importantly, Your Honours, you should take their word for it. We submit that is a not a proper standard under Rule 98 bis, that they are required to evidence. Their failure to demonstrate evidence requires dismissal of those charges and we invite the Trial Chamber to follow the guidance given by the Trial Chamber in Oric with respect to partial dismissal of murder allegations. With respect to the necessary and reasonable measures, again, we heard, for example, about Grahovo, ignoring various evidence in the record, which I will not go into detail on. However, suffice it to say, that P71 reflects, at page 48, orders to shoot at the legs of persons, burning and looting. It reflects the fact that Minister Susak, this is at page 73, was personally advised of crimes in Grahovo. And as the Court knows, the military police was under the command of the Ministry of Defence, meaning the minister of Defence, and then General Lausic under his command. And we know from P71, page 69, that General Gotovina determined that the problem was a lack of discipline in OG North. And at D793, on the 2nd of August, he replaces the commander of OG North and appoints General Ademi. The Prosecution in its convoluted conspiracy theory suggests that orders given after -- before, during and after Operation Storm were "empty orders," yet what were they unable to rebut? We put forward in our presentation that as of the 18th August, after the measures taken on that date, there is no further evidence of any information going to the Split Military District Command that General Gotovina's orders were ineffective, or that any units in the Split Military District were engaging in criminal activity on the territory of the Republic of Croatia. Mr. President, you asked me whether Mr. Theunens had testified as to whether it was in the -- specifically in the Split Military District diary, which is how I posed the question. You are correct. However, if you review the several pages before that, I put to him specifically whether there were any reports from political affairs, SIS, et cetera. He said he needed time during the break to review the material and when he returned he did not offer any such evidence. I submit that you were present and know that Mr. Theunens had no problem interjecting his own evidence if he felt it necessary. And more importantly, the Prosecution had the opportunity yesterday to refute my -- or our position that there is no such evidence. Accordingly, the suggestion that there was -- there weren't necessary and reasonable measures taken is refuted by the evidence. To suggest that demobilisation was a reckless measure is pure testimony given by counsel here. They adduced no evidence to that fact. The only evidence in the record on that issue is from Prosecution witness Lausic, Exhibit P2159, paragraph 210, where Mr. Lausic said the strongest way to deal with an undisciplined reserve would be the threat of demobilisation. The Prosecution had the opportunity to challenge Mr. Lausic on that point, to challenge Ms. Botteri on that point, to ask Mr. Theunens whether he agreed on that point. Most importantly, they had General Pringle on their witness list, and at the end of the day decided not to call him. The Prosecution's case at the 98 bis stage is left with the Prosecution trial counsel offering their own "expert opinion" as to whether demobilisation was a sufficient measure. We submit at 98 bis, that doesn't work for the Prosecution. Mr. President, Your Honours, I know I'm out of time so let me wrap up by saying that there is simply no evidence from which this Trial Chamber could conclude that there is sufficient evidence in the record that could rise to the level of proof beyond a reasonable doubt of the allegations made by the Prosecution in their case in-chief. In light of all of evidence that they have failed to adduce or have failed to confront, we submit that drawing inferences against specific evidence in the record is also something that the Appeals Chamber has indicated is not an appropriate way to convict the accused, and we accordingly ask for the entry of a Rule 98 bis order dismissing all counts. Thank you, Your Honours, and I thank you for the extra time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. We will have a break. After the break, Mr. Kuzmanovic, by the way, welcome. I promised that I would welcome you. You will be the third one and will it Mr. Kay second?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And thank you for the welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a break and we'll resume at 25 minutes to 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, on behalf of Mr. Cermak, we shall answer each and every point raised by the Prosecution in their submissions to the Court in turn. The first matter that Your Honours were referred to in the Prosecution address on the Rule 98 bis hearings was the relevant indicators of effective control. The first matter raised by Mr. Margetts was the procedure used for the appointment of an accused. I refer the Court to Exhibit P1187, Law on Service in the Armed Forces, Article 159, "appointments of senior officers and generals shall be the responsibility of the Supreme Commander." Proceeding now to the next matter. Reliance was placed upon Exhibits D561, and Exhibit 1219, P1219, reports to the chief of the Main Staff. If we look at these documents, there is not a plurality as implied in the submission but there was one issue arising from Exhibit D561, when the chief of Main Staff, General Cervenko, wrote to the commanders of Military Districts and included the Knin garrison, as well as the intelligence administration and others, for information, and that's what this document amounts to, not tactical orders or any orders of command. It was for information. And how did General Cermak respond to this? One could say not in the fullest way. When one looks at Exhibit P1219, the Split Military District Command and Knin garrison are in constant coordination. No information was actually provided by General Cermak. To set that against another document in evidence, Exhibit D564, the report from the Gospic Military District, indicating what was done by them. In fact, Your Honours, we submit that this is a classic example which shows the Defence submissions as being correct, that General Cermak was not commanding or operational, and the fact no report was filed by him actually indicates he had no effective control. We're grateful for the Prosecution arguments on this matter. Why was this sent? Probably the President's visit on the 26th of August, when he was arriving by train to Knin. The next matter raised as a relevant indicator was contact with President Tudjman and Mr. Jarnjak. How does that show effective control on the ground? The quality of the contact should be the issue. And before we look that, the word "contact" in itself is interesting, because it does not indicate a formal reporting structure or commanding system, but the only phrase that can be served is in itself of a non-operational nature, the word "contact." And the interesting feature of this argument is that if General Cermak was going to the minister of the interior and the President, asking for more police, and asking for more troops, that indicates he had no effective control in his position. And he wasn't able to submit a formal report. He was not able to go through a formal command structure. He was using his contacts. Influence is not enough in these cases. Mr. Flynn said he believed he was influential. And so he might have been. And using that influence for the good was not a bad thing. What this indicates is that General Cermak was taking positive and appropriate action outside his position to try and deal with crimes and problems in the liberated area. Consider his interview, as the Prosecution asked, page 2122 of the 1998 interview. This indicates he had no effective control, as these were measures he could not take himself. Not only that. Consider transcript page 5731, when Mr. Jarnjak is contacted, when he protects Witness 86 and supports him. The fact that this situation occurred at all indicates that General Cermak was supportive of law and order, contrary to the JCE. Furthermore, the fact that there was this argument concerning how events had occurred at Grubori indicates that General Cermak in the military was not involving himself in a civil police matter. I asked the Court to look at Exhibit P957, an example, again, of contact. When one looks at this document, and I am looking at page 2, the bottom of it, an example of General Cermak contacting the minister of internal affairs and asking him to contact the civil police in Split to establish coordination, to avoid accidents in future of internationals having their freedom of movement restricted. That indicates, again, no effective control, because if he was in control, he could have contacted the civil police in Split himself. The next matter raised was the authority to apply disciplinary measures. The case of Strugar was cited, paragraphs 393 to 397. Again, we're grateful to the Prosecution. It was an authority we had cited in our address to the Court, and it precisely demonstrates General Cermak has no effective control. This authority here concerns subordination of units and the authority to give direct combat orders, which General Cermak certainly did not have. And the Court is welcome to look at the details within those paragraphs of the authority. The service regulations, Exhibit D32, Article 52, were cited as being an example of disciplinary measures. In our submission, these rules go to something entirely different. These concern rules by which the military should conduct itself in a garrison town exactly as agreed by the Prosecution expert, Mr. Theunens, in cross-examination through me, transcript page 12881 to 4. And D32 has to be considered in the context of the later order of 1993, the order concerning organisation regarding work, order, and discipline at garrison headquarters. Exhibit D34, paragraph 2 of which says: "Garrison headquarters commands do not have an operational function and the right to issue orders to Croatian army units except precisely prescribed authorities regarding work, order and discipline at the garrison." To borrow an expression from my learned friend, Mr. Cayley, the Prosecution dance on a pinhead. They don't seek to provide information outside that pinhead and to give the Court the full context and picture. Let us turn now to the next of the relevant indicators relied upon. The reality of authority of the accused, his rank and he knew and was trusted by the President. This observation must be made. The fact that the President has contact with Mr. Cermak, as he was, and then General Cermak, as he was mobilised on the 5th of August, is not of itself significant. A president would have contact with many people. This does not answer any question of effective control. The evidence still has to be assessed; and in our submission, all descriptions of General Cermak's tasks were those of a non-operational, normalisation of life character. All the presidential transcripts that have been produced in this court do not in any way undermine that submission, and we will be looking, in particular, at the one from 1999 later in this submission. The next matter that was relied upon by the Prosecution were the assessments of General Cermak's authority, first of all, by the international witnesses. We do not dispute that the international witnesses had their beliefs about what General Cermak was able to do and what his position was. The issues in this court are whether those assessments were right, and we submit that we have proven during the course of the Prosecution case that the foundation of their assessments was based solely upon impression. Let us look just at a few passages of evidence. Exhibit P147, page 5, produced through the witness Ermolaev. Summary of meetings. At the headquarters of General Gotovina, as the headquarters of General Gotovina is in Knin, and also the headquarters of General Cermak, who deals with the non-operational matters, CALO, and the majority of his team has to stay obviously permanently in Knin. The witness Flynn, who was one of the first Prosecution witnesses and who had made a statement for the Prosecutor, giving his opinion and impressions conceded, transcript page 1086, he did not know what Mr. Cermak's job was. Exhibit P361, the Forand cable of 9th of August in which he says at paragraph 1C: "Croatian army units deny Cermak's authority and even his existence." Exhibit P375, another General Forand letter: "Cermak frustrated with his authority and limited in certain areas." A very important letter from that witness, because it was clear that he was speaking in a way that showed that he was pleased with the level of cooperation of General Cermak. Transcript page 1176 to 7. Mr. Flynn never believed General Cermak had direct command and responsibility over units. You can display impression evidence from either side. This Court should be concerned with the foundation of evidence. It is not good enough just to rely upon impressions. And if impressions are contradicted, we submit it is the duty of the Court to accept the actuality, the reality. Transcript page 1183 to 4. Mr. Flynn never believed General Cermak was in control of the police. I could go on with other references; I will not. Looking at it from another pair of eyes, General Leslie, transcript page 2202 to 3. The only information he had about General Cermak was from the UN system. The Court will remember that there was evidence of General Forand writing on the 5th of August to be directed to the military governor. This was a perception of General Cermak that had been built up in advance through Western eyes and to a position that did not exist. Transcript page 2200 to 1. General Leslie did not know tasks and responsibilities of General Cermak and never saw him command troops. Witness Berikoff, transcript page 7821 to 2. They all relied on the rank, uniform, title, which was conceded by him as being incorrect. In support of this, the Prosecution have sought to use the testimony of a so-called insider witness, described as being consistent and corroborative of their argument, the witness Buhin. He had never met General Cermak; transcript page 1007. He didn't know Mr. Dondo, the lieutenant who has featured in this case. He didn't know what General Cermak's job was, but he knew it concerned coordination. Let us turn now to de facto and de jure authority that the Prosecution cited as being significant and indicative of the authority of General Cermak. Cited in support of this was Exhibit D32, the service regulations. We've looked at those already. This proposition would give the garrison commander control over all the units within a garrison at the expense of the operational commanders. It simply doesn't make sense. Look at Mr. Theunens's testimony, transcript page 12290 to 91. There are simply no orders and evidence to support that General Cermak had de facto and de jure authority over all the units within the Split Military District. This one regulation involving specific powers of the garrison has been used in a way that is like dancing on a pinhead, and in our submission does not look at the substance of this case, we invite the Court to do. Paragraph 1(E) of Exhibit D33, which defines the area of the garrison, is relied upon. Interesting in the language of that document which just sets out the municipalities, it refers to the tasks of the garrison, not command. Consider also Exhibit D818, a letter which tells General Cermak not to issue international passes, a non-operational matter, showing that he had to restrict any steps taken by him in relation to areas where there was a so-called war zone. This emphasised the non-operational tasks that he had to perform. The next heading relied upon was the ability to initiate investigations into the conduct and discipline soldiers in the units using military police and civilian police. There is absolutely no evidence to support the proposition that General Cermak had a duty to investigate. The Court has been referred to the Code of Military Discipline and his responsibility to discipline his own subordinates; Article 19. They numbered nine, and indeed, only to deal with minor disciplinary breaches under Article 26. Now, there is an clear hierarchy structure in this system. It is not a system that the Prosecution would have to accept would be the governing system, if their arguments and propositions were to be supported. Consider his interview in 1998, page 30, when he said he had no power to issue orders to troops and units. Witness 86, transcript page 5706, lines 9 to 19, Cermak couldn't order investigations. For other references of Cermak being unable to issue orders to the police, see transcript pages 5555 - four 5s, that is - to 7. 5684, 5688, 5691, and 5696. I forecast to the Court that I would return to the witness Buhin, whom the Prosecution described as consistent and corroborative. He described General Cermak at transcript page 10044, as being a role of coordination, looking after life and work in the liberated area, generally speaking. At transcript page 10046, he knew he was a commander in Knin, not privy to the detail. He was asked: "Did you know enough to give your opinion? " "Answer: No." That question was asked as a result of the witness statement that has been taken from this witness and put in evidence under Rule 92 ter. In our submission, significant problems have been thrown up in this case by the use of those statements because the full context of evidence was never being put to the witnesses. I referred the Court in my first address to the fact that the so-called MUP, UNCRO military police orders were not put before witnesses. Transcript page 9977, Cermak had no authority to issue orders to the civilian police. We got orders from the MUP. And that was how the system worked and how the documents and paper trail in this case show the system working. The Court would have to find that all those documents that we have been looking at existed for naught, and people actioning each other with their own lines of authority were actually under the command and control of a person utterly outside the system. The witness Dzolic, transcript page 8929, lines 17 to 21: "Cermak couldn't order me." Transcript page 9017, lines 13 to 18: "Cermak had no authority to order you to investigate crimes," I asked. He agreed: "That is right." Transcript page 9027, line 24: "I was not obliged to follow orders of this kind as orders." Transcript page 9037, line 1 to 13: "... not under the command of General Cermak. Wrong to say he was to obey any order." The phrase in the witness statement came in via 92 ter and demonstrating a significant lack of context and, indeed, penetration as to important issues of subordination and effective command. I will not go further into anything of dual command because, in my submission, it simply wasn't relevant nor being raised by me. Witness P84. He'd never seen orders by General Cermak to the Knin police; transcript page 1137 to 8. And they weren't put to him in his statement. Furthermore, there were two documents underlying the UNCRO orders, in which he referred to a complaint being made by the commander of the Knin garrison. In our submission, all this evidence and all these factors utterly contradict the slenderest of lines used by the Prosecution to put forward an argument of effective control. It was suggested that General Cermak had command over troops in the operational zone. The document being relied upon was Exhibit P390, freedom of movement document, dated 11th of August; and a letter to General Cermak -- from General Cermak to General Forand, allowing full freedom of movement for the UN. And you look carefully at this document, Exhibit P390, and it's delivered to troops in zone of separation, whatever that means, and to the Croatian Ministry of Defence, UN, and EU office. At the 1998 interview, pages 59 to 60, Mr. Cermak said: "I would phone them and tell them to tell their units on the ground that people had freedom of movement." Interestingly enough, he couldn't contact the units himself, but as he said, he was contacting to enable other units to tell their units on the ground. Well, no military system with effective control vested in a general could operate like that. Interestingly enough, the witness Berikoff described the letter by General Cermak as a joke; transcript page 7791 to 2. General Forand said: "It wasn't of any help. There was still problems, as it wasn't always recognised." Transcript page 4317. Exhibit P375, General Forand refers to the limit of authority, and in evidence described General Cermak as a conduit. There were many more references to how the police, army did not respect Cermak's orders. Hill, transcript 3799. Also consider these pages with other witnesses, transcript 133 to 4; 1176 to 7; transcript 1251, and that will be enough now. The orders allegedly acted upon to demonstrate authority were cited as Exhibits P509, Exhibit P510 and Exhibit D303. Witness 86 did not take that as an order; transcript 5696. Witness Buhin said not an order; transcript 9977. Also look at Exhibits D494, 495, 496, where the civilian police consider the Cermak passes and try to fathom what is happening as to whether they are valid or not. The eventual conclusion at Exhibit D496 is that it was said to be only for the Ministry of Defence and not civilians. The system in operation contradicts the Prosecution case in theory. Taking Exhibit D303, there is the paper trail of exhibits submitted by the Defence to show the failure to collect/track the UNCRO vehicles, requiring intervention; Exhibit P391, D503, D304, D500, D501, D305, and D306. Reliance was made on the presidential transcript, Exhibit P1144, to somehow link General Cermak with Generals Norac and Gotovina, and it is clear from the terms of the exhibits that all three had been questioned or sought to be questioned or were to be -- charges were to be brought against them in the content of the transcript; page 7: "They are going to bring charges against the three of us, aren't they?" The talk is about the three. Cermak saying, This is all perfect nonsense, saying they were innocent, none of us ordered any killing, rubbish. Norac and Gotovina were conducting military operations. They were in command of military actions. And now let's go to the full terms not read out by the Prosecution. "I was in command of my part," and there it stopped. So what was his part? "After two days, we set up a soup kitchen, which was visited both by Croats and by Serbs." We engaged ourselves in humanitarian work; made tours to the villages; set up power units; we have more than enough papers and stories for them. As for incidents in the field, no one could have prevented them. You, President, you had a situation with the fighters in the field. Well, if you are having a conversation about effective authority and you're referring to soup kitchens and the like, in our submission, the underlying bedrock of evidence presented by the Defence in this case is -- is plainly supported by unarranged, unplanned conversations at the time. Notice of crimes. Exhibit P918 was relied upon by the Prosecutor. And the Court knows that General Cermak never denied crimes. He may have had differences of opinion concerning what caused them. He never denied that they were happening. And in our submission, this document, Exhibit P918, dated the 12th of August, being a warning from the political affairs section, sent only for information to the commander of Knin garrison indicates that General Cermak had correctly passed on and reported all those incidents that had been raised to him by General Forand and others in the days from the 8th of August until this time. "You know that General Forand had said about looting, burning crimes, because this document refers to the fact that the international community could undertake measures which would have unforeseeable consequences for our state." Well, information passed on by General Cermak results in the warning; and for information, that document has been sent to him because he was the one, General Forand. See the exhibit of his letter on the 11th of August where he said that Croatia would be liable for destruction and thefts. I'm sorry I can't give the Court the exhibit number for that, but maybe we will be able to in the interim period. Moving on to the next subject, Mr. Hayden, bringing in a meeting to General Cermak's attention problems in the region and that people were killed. Prosecutor say that Mr. Cermak was misleading. There's no evidence of that at all. He handed over reports that enabled Mr. Hayden and his colleagues to do an analysis. If he was misleading them as to the nature of deaths and who was killed, why would he have handed over reports that they could analyse? In our submission, steps taken by him to assist and help the international community at the time are wrongfully being attacked as examples of conduct which do not make sense in an analysis of the evidence. He was a conduit for that information. What's happening here in this example and the other examples is that the messenger is being shot. Don't shoot the messenger is the important principle. Let me turn now, in the last ten minutes, to matters raised in the submissions of my learned friend on Grubori. One factor needs to be made clear. This was a matter entirely within the province of the civil police from beginning to end, the MUP. Cermak had no authority or right to issue or institute a police investigation. Witness 86 confirmed; transcript page 5706. Remember the sequence of events. The 25th of August was the date when Grubori happened. The garrison was contacted, not General Cermak, but the office. The first report filed was one of fires. The internationals went back to the scene and arrived after 6.00 and then learnt of deaths. That night, the internationals did not go back to the garrison. Neither did they go to the Knin police to report to the local police that this was not now a situation of burning but was one of deaths. The next information that came to General Cermak was on the 26th of August, and we can look at Exhibit P504, the transcript of the UNTV interview at 11.00 in the morning. General Cermak repeatedly said he did not know of the events concerning killings. He was only aware of events that happened yesterday, and he gave information that was known by him at that stage. It is clear from the interviews he had been in contact, or had been contacted by, the special police who had given information to him. See Exhibit P579 for corroboration of the fact of a body being found with wire and hands tied behind the back. General Cermak was repeatedly pressed many times to investigate this matter. He would -- he had said he would verify the matter, but the question of an investigation was an issue created by the questioner. There is no evidence at this time as to what information was exactly in his possession, but we can take it from the progress of the interview that it was clear at that stage he did not know about deaths until the interviewer himself said two civilians had been killed. That also was not the full account, because we know, in fact, that more people had been killed. From the terms of this interview, you can quite clearly see that General Cermak had said that the civil police had been to the village and were unable to see anything. We know from the evidence of Witness 86 that that is correct. The system was actually working as it should. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Lieutenant Dondo wrote on the 26th of August, with no findings, an interim report as to what he had seen up there and passed on the information. Exhibit P764, second page, paragraph 5 in the English. This is a very telling paragraph as to how the Knin garrison operated. They were promised that the bodies would most probably be cleared up on the 27th of August. You make a promise if someone asks you to do something, and that representatives of civilian structures would come to help them with accommodation since their houses had been burned down. This garrison wasn't operating as some clearing house for a joint criminal enterprise. This garrison was operating on a humanitarian basis, as described, and taking appropriate measures to ensure, so far as they could, that people were helped. This is an internal memo, not a memo for public consumption, so this memo provides a snapshot of how General Cermak tried to run the affairs of the garrison in Knin at this time. When one moves to what happened later in this account, it is quite clear Witness 86 said that General Cermak did not seek to obstruct the investigation; he was supportive to the witness, to the minister of the interior. If he was a man part of this joint criminal enterprise, why on earth would he be behaving supportively to Witness 86? Not only that, he was letting him do his business and a more senior police officer, a man called Sacic, from the special police, a direct senior within the hierarchy of the Ministry of Interior, was the man who was attempting to obstruct and prevent. In our submission, it is quite clear that General Cermak was entitled to rely upon the police handling a non-military matter that had been brought to his attention but was not a matter over which he had command and control, and the steps taken were entirely appropriate in the circumstances.
