utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is our 98 bis submission in response to what the Prosecution has put forth yesterday. It is going to come in two parts, Your Honours. The first part will discuss the -- what has been termed the unlawful artillery attack on Gracac and Donji Lapac that was addressed mostly by Mr. Russo. The second part will deal with the 7(3) liability, which was dealt with primarily by Ms. Mahindaratne. At the outset, the Court needs to be aware, and I'm sure the Court is aware, that in terms of planning, General Markac had no role in planning Operation Storm. He was used as an implementation -- in implementation of Operation Storm, and I would like to advise the Court -- and if we could pull up D535, which is map. Your Honours, D535 is the map that was provided to General Markac, and the special police referred to in another exhibit -- or in this same exhibit, in which the special police was supposed to -- which was supposed to, on this axis of attack, cut the road off between Gospic and Gracac and go towards Gracac and take various military objectives from the Velebit mountains. Now on the English version of this document, the map on the bottom right states the HV General Staff order addressed to commander of MUP special units, General Mladen Markac, signed by Janko Bobetko. Now D535 itself, is the order of General Bobetko, and this map was provided, among other things, to General Markac. Why is this an important issue with respect to planning? If we take a look at P614, page 2 -- D535, by the way, was in June of 1995, obviously before the Brioni meeting. Nothing changed through July of 1995 in terms of what was eventually required of the special police under the Main Staff of the Croatian military. If we look at page 3 of P614, it says: "On 29 July 1995" -- We don't necessarily need it up on the screen, Mr. Registrar, that's fine. "The HV GS HQ," which is the Croatian military General Staff headquarters. "A written order was issued to the leadership of the special police sector with a map marked up with the attack axes and the joint special forces zone of responsibility relating to the assault operation and the capture of the Mali Alan pass and the Celavac radio relay centre, cutting the Sveti Rok-Gracac road, as well as overrunning the general Sveta Ruka and Sveti Rok area in the three days of the operation." Now what does P614 tell us? It tells that, first of all, General Markac was not involved in planning Operation Storm. Second of all, his axis of attack through the Velebit mountains was initially to go to just outside of Gracac to cut that road. Now, why is this important? When we look back at the artillery issue, we see that the entire area at or near the Mali Alan pass and further in that axis of attack is uninhabited. There is no civil population there. It is entirely an area where the military was located; that is the ARSK military. There were heavy battles in those areas, and you will see when you refer to some of the UNMO reports, specifically P102 in which it discusses on the first day of Operation Storm how the Mali Alan pass was taken by the special police well on their way on -- to the second day on their way to Gracac. Now, what happened with respect to the claim of an unlawful artillery attack on Gracac and Donji Lapac - thank you, Your Honour - which allegedly caused the civilian population to leave? If we look at the testimony of Mr. Kosta Novakovic, transcript references 11729 and 11815, at 11729, on the evening of August 4th, this is well before the special police even were close to coming to Gracac, Mr. Novakovic testified that -- that they decided to evacuate the population out of Dalmatia, Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Drnis, and out of the Gracac municipality and Lika. Why? Because there was the danger that practically across Mali Alan the route would be cut off, which was the only route leading toward the hinterland, via Otocac and Dalmatia. The entire army and the entire population would find themselves encircled. If we go to 11815 at line 5, it says: "When the civilian protection organs had conveyed the decision to their commissioners in those four municipalities in Dalmatia, and Gracac municipality, then that decision, evacuation order, was no longer a secret." And the question is asked: "Then in fact at some point you are aware that the evacuation decision did get into the media on the evening of the 4th; correct? "Answer: Absolutely, yes." Now, why is this important? Because, Your Honours, by the time the special police got to Gracac, the city was empty. There were battles that went on leading up to Gracac, but when they got to Gracac, the city was empty. Now what kind of shape was the city in as a result of this allegedly unlawful artillery attack? First of all, I need to correct something that Mr. Russo said regarding Mr. Janic. Mr. Janic was not the leader of the axis of attack with respect to Gracac. His transcript reference regarding his axis of attack is on page 6392, lines 16 through 18. He says: "Mr. Janic you testified about artillery support that you asked for during the course of the attack. Now you said that there were predetermined targets. There were any predetermined targets in civilian populated areas in your line of attack? "Answer: No, there weren't. Which stage are we talking it? The first stage of Operation Storm or the entire operation?" The question is: "Operation Storm, the first stage, on 4th and 5th August." And here is where he describes his line of attack: "My line of attack was Velebit, Celavac up until Prezid, so up the road -- up until the road. This was an uninhabited area. There weren't even villages in that area in my line of attack. Apart from the first and second enemy lines, and up to the Celavac repeater, there were no other facilities. There were no other buildings, so there weren't any targets, targets that you are referring to now." He is further asked about the issue of targeting, and he says later on in that same transcript reference: "The predetermined targets were the enemy positions and the depth of their defence line, the artillery positions, their command post, their depots, the targets, where the enemy infrastructure that they used to defend their lines. Those were the exclusive targets that we had. Whenever conducting an operation, well, it wasn't possible to have any other targets. All the targets were military targets. The purpose was to break through the enemy defence line and to attain the operation's objective. It wasn't possible to have any other objective." There is some discussion about targeting in civilian populated areas regarding Mr. Rajcic and Mr. Janic and we can see from Mr. Janic's testimony that there was no targeting of civilian populated areas. If we again look at Mr. Janic's testimony -- actually, I already discussed Mr. Janic's testimony relating to targeting. What I wanted to discuss is the UNMO report, P102, of August 4th which reported 15 shells in the area of Gracac, which is exactly the same number of shells that Mr. Sovilj discussed, which is very close to the number of shells Mr. Turkalj discussed. And if we look at P111, on page 3, the only UNMO assessment done of shelling damage with respect to Gracac said that the main artillery impacts in Gracac were on the main junction. So, with respect to an alleged unlawful artillery attack on Gracac, Your Honours, it doesn't exist. By the time the special police reached Gracac, according to the evacuation order issued as discussed by Mr. Novakovic, the civilian population was gone. I'd like to talk a bit about the issue of forward observers. There's a discussion of forward observers that Mr. Russo discusses and the fact that the special police allegedly had no forward observers, and that's really not exactly what the testimony was. Let's look at the testimony of Mr. Turkalj. That's at transcript reference 13695, pages 5 to 20 -- lines 5 to 22: "So your testimony is there were no forward observers. So in the absence of forward observers, who corrected the fire for you? "Answer: Let me answer this way: Along the axis of attack of the special police it is true that the commanders of the units sought -- sought support from their battery and all -- and they all had had a coded map based on which they were able to pinpoint the exact location of a target. Specifically when they came into contact with the enemy and when they engaged in combat, based on the coded map, they would -- they would not" -- I would presume that means they would know, "exactly where they were and where the target was, and then they would ask for the support from their battery which would fire at the target. Of course, they were able to adjust their fire if it was closer, further away, to the left, or to the right. Let me just add, the artillery batteries were not able to have their own observers or spotters because the terrain would not allow for that but the commanders of units or, rather, commanders of specific axes were also observers." Now the next line I think is very telling: "Why didn't the terrain allow for forward observers." And the answer was a little bit sarcastic but it's true: "I suppose you didn't see the area. It's a mountain." Now, the fact that the artillery batteries did not have their own individual forward observers is irrelevant because the commanders on the ground had a coded map in which they would be able to pinpoint targets to call in to the batteries to have accurate artillery fire. There is absolutely no dispute. So the fact that there is no separate forward observer for an artillery battery with respect to the special police area of operations is completely irrelevant. Let's look at the next issue discussed, specifically looting, which was supposedly attributed to in the Plavno valley and in Orlic. And as a citation, the Prosecution in its presentation uses two exhibits. One exhibit is P1249. Now, I have checked the transcript twice and I put that number into e-court and that -- nothing shows up so I don't know if 1249 is mistransposed. I don't know if 1249 actually exists, about as far as I'm concerned, that's a non-issue. The next document that's cited is P267. P267 is a five-page document dated September 29th of 1995, from UNCIVPOL. Nowhere in P267 is the word "Orlic" contained; nowhere in P267 is the special police specifically mentioned at any point. Now, I think the Prosecution with respect to the special police has a fundamental misunderstanding about what kind of territorial control the special police had. It had none. It was not a Military District, like Split or Gospic; there is no evidence that the special police operated in any way on a territorial basis, other than having an axis of attack; and there's no evidence anywhere that General Markac was ordered to take control of the territory that he and his forces liberated. Now we left off at Gracac. Before the special police got to Gracac, there is a claim that General Markac ordered Gracac to be taken. However, D550 and D551, are both orders from the -- from the Chief of Staff, General Cervenko, of the Main Staff of the Croatian military, that order General Markac to continue his attack, one, through Gracac; and two, on to Donji Lapac, all the way to the state border. General Markac did not do this on his own. He was ordered to do so by the Main Staff. Now, there was an intensive large movement of men and materiel going on that road from Gospic to Donji Lapac. Those men and materiel, other than being military for the most part, also included civilians. However, when you look at the UNMO reports, P108, P109, and P110. P108 is an UNMO report which is dated the 6th of August, the Jordanian battalion which was at or near Donji Lapac, in Boricevac, reported that there were ten ARSK tanks, followed by 200 soldiers heading to Bosnia. P109, also the 6th of August. On the first page, the ARSK continued to depart to Bosnia. On the second page, significantly it says: "The general area of Donji Lapac, as assessed, is still under RSK control." Now, this is the day before the special police went on to liberate Donji Lapac. In this same report the Jordanian battalion again, located in Boricevac, not far from Donji Lapac, ARSK convoy of 15 trucks pulling guns, one bus with 200 personnel observed heading to Bosnia at Boricevac border check-point. Another entry, ARSK convoy, 150 personnel on six trucks towing two guns headed to Bosnia. Again, 6th of August at 1115, ten ARSK tanks, 200 soldiers with individual weapons headed to Bosnia. And what do we see at the bottom here on this same page of P109, which is the fifth page: "UNMO Team Gracac met with the commander of HV special forces and allowed to carry out patrol in Gracac." P110, here's where we discuss the issue of Donji Lapac. I'm going transition now to Donji Lapac. This is the UNMO report. First page dated 7th of August. HV artillery shelled Donji Lapac from Udbina. Now, that's not the axis of operation from which the special police came. Udbina is assessed to be taken by HV troops. RD preparation for further attack on Donji Lapac. Further on in the same exhibit, UNMO Team Gracac reported freedom of movement between Gracac and Gospic, and I referred to this earlier. UNMO team discovered that the main RD impacts on 4 August was around main junction. If we look further next on the next page, the Jordanian battalion again. HV artillery shelled Donji Lapac from Udbina. And again extensive artillery shelling against Donji Lapac. The same date, August 10th, on the way, in the same general area of Donji Lapac, ten ARSK trucks carrying 100 persons arrived at border platoon in Donji Lapac area and started harassing and asking for fuel and rations. This is after the special police in Donji Lapac left the area. So you can see that in Donji Lapac and the vicinity there was a heavy presence of Serb military, as reported by the United Nations military observers, and the shelling that occurred in Donji Lapac was not from the special police, but came from Udbina which was not in the special police axis of attack. Now, with respect to Donji Lapac, neither the special police or General Markac were in Donji Lapac on August 6th as was -- as was argued yesterday. The special police entered Donji Lapac on August 7th, and set up on the outskirts of Donji Lapac and left for Kulen Vakuf on the border -- near the border with Bosnia on the morning of the 8th. I cite for reference P585, P470, P586, and P556. One other reference that I forgot to add with respect to Donji Lapac and the UNMO report, P114, was that on the 10th of August at Donji Lapac, the UNMO observed soldiers wearing BiH insignia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, helping refugees from Bihac with trucks to collect cows and other household items left behind by the Krajina Serbs. Let's go over P585 for a moment. But before I do that, Your Honours, I wanted to refer to Janic's testimony again with respect to the road between Gracac and Donji Lapac and the fact that the Serbian military there was entering into a fighting -- was -- was engaging in a fighting withdrawal. On page 6391 of the transcript, Mr. Janic was asked: "While that you were advancing toward Otric and further beyond to Lapac and Gornji Vakuf, did you see damaged and abandoned vehicles beside the road and equipment as well? "Answer: Yes, we did. On each of these roads while we were advancing during the operation, we saw broken vehicles or destroyed vehicles and weapons that were left behind while they were fleeing. "Question: Did you notice particularly at road junctions any traces of firing from artillery, and I mean tanks and guns. Did you see any shell casings by the road while you were travelling towards Otric and further beyond towards Lapac? "Answer: Yes. On several places we saw traces of their artillery positions. We found empty shells after they had been firing from artillery and that happened on several occasions along the road." So during the course of the special police's activity along its axis of operations on the way to Donji Lapac there was evidence obviously of a fighting withdrawal. If you look at P85, as I was discussing earlier -- P585, excuse me. It's a report dated the 8th of August, signed by General Markac, which described that, on 7 August 1995, along with rocket artillery support and the usage of armour, special police joined forces, seized the village of Mazin, Dobro Selo, Gornji Lapac, Donji Lapac, and after the reached line, they regrouped and started a quick break-through towards the state border and the Una river with the purpose to liberate Kulen Vakuf." Now, if you look at P586, again another reference used regarding Lapac. P586 is a -- is a 2 October 1995 letter from Mr. Branislav Bole [phoen] of the special police. This letter says in part: "On 7 August, during the liberation of Donji Lapac by joint forces of the special police, around 1600 hours logistics support entered and stationed itself in the town centre. Although in Donji Lapac there were no greater battles in the town centre, two houses were burning as a consequence of artillery rocket support actions." In the eve of the same day from the direction of Udbina, the 9th Guards Brigade and -- with tanks and the 118th Home Guard regiment arrived. Upon entry of the above said units, the town -- in town, shooting from infantry weapons started, throwing of bombs, setting houses on fire, which continued the entire night. The chief of the anti-terrorist section, Mr. Zdravko Janic, spoke with Colonel Brajkovic and the officers of the 118th about calming of the situation in town. They promised that they would solve that. However, the situation did not significantly improve during the night. The special police forces did not take part in fire-starting in Donji Lapac. And this is a document cited by the Prosecution that the special police participated in the destruction of Donji Lapac. It is entirely the opposite. Now let's look at the third document that is referred to there, P556. D556, excuse me. D556, again, dated September 10th. This is from Mr. Janic. In the middle of this document, it says: "While entering and liberating Donji Lapac, special police forces," on August 7th, by the way, 1995, "special police forces did not engage in larger combats so the town was preserved in entirety. In the town itself, in the moment when our troops entered, only two larger facilities in the very centre were on fire when shot by our artillery. After entering Donji Lapac, special police forces did not stay there but they have taken defensive positions around the town itself and on its border areas while only logistics stayed in the town." Again, consistent with the previous exhibit, between 5.00 and 6.00 p.m., HV troops came to Donji Lapac from the direction of Udbina, 9th Guards Brigade and the 118th. Again, consistent with the other document, while the aforementioned forces were entering the town, general shooting began, hand-grenades were thrown, to burning houses and facilities in Donji Lapac. "Around 6.00 p.m., I," meaning Janic, "spoke to Colonel Brajkovic and an unnamed officer of the 118th trying to calm down the situation in town, to stop burning and shooting. Special police forces, who were on their defensive positions around and on border areas of Donji Lapac, did not participate in shooting and burning." You can also look, Your Honours, at P2166, page 35, and English page 39 which is General Lausic's diary, which does not attribute what happened in Donji Lapac to the special police. Let's look at P470, a presidential transcript. This is cited as evidence that the special police destroyed Donji Lapac. Page 54 of P470. This is -- by the way, page 53 has been cited I don't know how many times by the Prosecution with respect to Mr. Susak's comment about the -- everything is destroyed. The next page, Mr. Norac says: "Mr. President, when entering the town, the units were caught by night, Storm and shooting, and everything was burnt down during that night. First, the special police entered. There was a big fire after that. That part could not be controlled anymore, while in this other part everything remained." This is cited as evidence that the special police burned down Donji Lapac. It's our submission that has absolutely nothing to do with the special police burning down Donji Lapac because it did not happen. There is nothing specific related to the special police about burning down the town, nothing specific about the special police shelling the town, there is no witness, no document, no exhibit that states that General Markac was ever in Donji Lapac during this time-frame. I'd like to refer for a moment to -- the issue regarding Konings. Mr. Konings doesn't address Donji Lapac. He doesn't address Gracac. The Prosecution did not make any response with respect to Konings on shelling issues relating to Donji Lapac or Gracac. The entire joint criminal enterprise claim against General Markac is summed up by Ms. Mahindaratne in a three-sentence quotation from a presidential transcript which in this context is entirely meaningless. P461, page 19, the quotation is this: "There is no change in the task except that Mr. Norac is heading upward. That means that we are going to drive them into a pocket here and from that point we can head towards Norac and while Norac can head towards Lapac and we have practically evacuated the entire area. Everything fits in, and to all practical purposes, we gain with this plan proposed by Mr. Gotovina." Now first reaction to that was: How in the world are those three sentences evidence of a joint criminal enterprise? There is no transcript reference for a discussion of shelling of civilians by General Markac. No order, no statement, no display of ethnic intolerance or hatred, no order for a crime, no plan for a crime, no enterprise at all, no comment, no intent, nothing. Briefly, mop-up operations, a claim that General Markac ordered them. This was ordered not by General Markac but by the chief of the Main Staff. Look at D561 as an example. Expert Theunens stated that mop-up operations were a legitimate military activity after Operation Storm, nothing inherently criminal or wrong or unlawful about them. I list a few things here that were unaddressed in the response. In the interests of time there are nine of them. First of all, there was no response this, that the special police had no territorial responsibility like the Military District of Split, like the Military District of Gospic. It had an axis of attack which was laid out and planned for it by the Main Staff of the Croatian military and by direct order from the Chief of Staff, General Cervenko. That's P614. Special police was not on the territory of Sector South after August 9th, when it was ordered to withdraw, again by the chief of the Main Staff, General Cervenko, in Exhibit D559, until August 21st when again the chief of the Main Staff, General Cervenko, ordered the special police to engage in specific mop-up operations; D561. During this time-frame the special police was not on the territory of Sector South. It was in Petrova Gora in Sector North. The Prosecution has not cited to a single eye-witness that any member of the special police was committing serious crimes, serious violations of international law, such as murder, harassment of civilians, wide-scale burning and looting, forcible displacement or unlawful detention of civilians. Not one single eye-witness. Four, in the police diaries which are in evidence from the police districts of Zadar, Gospic, Sibenik, and Split, there is not one entry that the Prosecution has produced in which any member of the special police is ever listed as being involved in any type of a crime. Five, in the joint meetings that are held between members of the Ministry of Interior, such as Mr. Moric and Mr. Benko, with General Lausic from the military police, with the civilian police coordinators, and government representatives posted in the newly liberated areas, the Prosecution has adduced no evidence of any crimes, isolated or widespread, committed by any member of the special police, nor is there any evidence produced of any notice, reporting, request, verbal or written, given to General Markac for any matter as a result of these joint meetings. Sixth, at all relevant times, with regard to entities responsible for the maintenance of law and order, the MUP regular police, the newly established police stations, Knin, Gracac, Donji Lapac, the Prosecution has adduced no evidence of crimes, isolated or widespread, committed by any member of the special police, nor is there any evidence produced of any notice, reporting, request, verbal or written, given to General Markac for any matter, any matter, as a result of the activities of the regular police, criminal police, investigating judge, or state prosecutor. Seven, General Lausic's testimony, from the side of the military police, contains no evidence where he ever refers to crimes committed by members of special police, nor does he report, written, verbal, or in any other fashion, of such alleged crimes to General Markac or any member of the special police. Eighth, there is never an order issued to General Markac from the Main Staff, or the Chief of Staff of the military, that the special police must stop people from its ranks from committing crimes, burning, looting, nor is there a report issued from any entity, civil or military, to the Main Staff reporting criminal acts being committed by members of the special police. Ninth, the Prosecution did not address in any way that the United Nations and the other internationals were totally and completely unprepared for what happened after Operation Storm. In many instances showing that they were not competent, incorrectly identifying uniformed personnel as members of the special police, and through their incorrect reporting, spreading this information everywhere. They were unable to correctly identify the following: The uniforms; the weapons, the type of vehicles; what the role was of the special police; what the structure was of the special police; who the leadership was of the special police; the fact that they did not hold check-points, which comes also from Lausic's evidence; and in fact the identity of the special police in areas which they never operated. I'd like to turn now to the issue of 7(3) liability. The first things I wanted to address is the claim that the special police were never given any instructions on how to obey -- that they should obey the international laws and rules of war. P552 is the statement of Mr. Janic. Paragraph 32 of that statement, which I will find in a moment, specifically discusses all of the things that they were instructed about. And I found it here. It says: "At our last meeting before the operation we were formally reminded of the international code of conduct of a war. All of our staff had been trained in the international rules of war before this operation, because we were expecting to have to handle prisoners of war and civilians. We were all reminded of these rules. We were also issued with a military booklet, which contained the international rules of war," and the paragraph goes on a little further. In the interests of time, I'm not going to read it. Now, the last area I want to cover is the measures and discipline that General Markac supposedly did not take. And the first issue I want to deal with is the issue of Ramljane. Now in Ramljane -- there are many exhibits that deal with Ramljane. The first several exhibits that deal with Ramljane are D563. D563 is the order regarding the freedom train involving a joint operation between the Croatian intelligence service, the military, the special police, the Home Guards and many others in which the special police was to provide security for the freedom train. If you look at Mr. Janic's testimony, and I'll just refer to the specific exhibits, P767 through 771 are all exhibits that deal with the investigation relating to Ramljane. Mr. Janic's testimony at 6193 discusses the issue of Ramljane, and on line 10 he says: "There was no doubt it was a conflict, a fighting, and that the burning was undoubtedly caused by the use of the hand-held rocket launchers. Therefore I had no doubts about the reports received from the commanders." General Markac asked Mr. Janic to look into Ramljane. He looked into Ramljane, and he reported on Ramljane. He did act, he did take measures, and you can see that through the documents that I have cited for the Court. Now let's look at the issue of Grubori as supposedly being notice for Ramljane. Grubori took place on the 25th; Ramljane took place on the 26th. No one had established that what happened in Grubori on the 25th or on the 26th. Let's look at the logic of what the Prosecution says was supposedly notice of a crime in Grubori as evidence of failure to take measures in Ramljane. Now, the first time the civilian police first found out about Grubori was on the 26th at 10.00 in the morning. On the 26th, as I documented, in Exhibit D563, the special police were already engaged in an operation for the freedom train near Ramljane. This order was issued on the 25th, the day before, for Ramljane. So General Markac is supposed to prevent some future conduct by someone he didn't know did anything wrong, for someone -- something he barely knew anything about, which happened less than 24 hours before Ramljane. That's not notice. That's actually absurd. Notwithstanding the fact that the witness Zganjer found no evidence anywhere of any kind of a cover-up, not one civilian or criminal police entity, while General Markac was in charge of the special police, ever sent him anything which would have enabled him to suspend anyone. I would encourage the Court, given my time, to look at one more exhibit relating to measures and look at -- with the context within which this -- these measures were taken, and that's D1079. General Markac took measures with respect to D1078 after he was informed by the competent criminal authorities that something had occurred. My learned colleague Mr. Kay discussed Grubori quite a bit. The only thing I would like to say about Grubori was that the Prosecution completely unaddressed -- did not address the issue of Mr. Zganjer's testimony, that he, as state prosecutor, found no evidence of a cover-up, and that Witness 84 said: "As the criminal police didn't do their job." The last thing I want to talk about with respect to Grubori is a document that the -- the Prosecution calls upon as "evidence," P505 [Realtime transcript read in error "pay 050"], unsigned, unnumbered, unstamped. Now, the fact that these documents in which General Markac supposedly wrote have differing versions of the events that occurred are attributable to the fact that he, as a commander, is entitled to rely on the information provided to him by his subordinates. That's the only way a commander can operate. And I submit to you, that had General Markac received something similar to what he received with respect to D1078, he would have done the same thing that did he in D1078. Your Honours, I would like to thank you for the opportunity to provide a response. I stayed within my time and I appreciate the Court's indulgence and we submit that under Rule 98 bis there is no evidence with respect to General Markac's criminal liability, either 7(1), 7(3) or JCE. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We should know -- P505 was not accurately designated in the transcript, just so you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn. Talking about accuracy or inaccuracy, Mr. Akhavan, as you may have noticed, and as most counsel do know, we try to follow you as closely as possible, you made a reference to the explanation given by the Oric Chamber on the meaning of 98 bis in its new formulation. You started quoting page 7857 and then you continued to -- and you made a reference to 7859, line 10, that's at least how it appears on the transcript. Now, I find a similar text and I must admit that I have not all the transcripts ready here, so I took the Internet version, I find something in relation to what you said in 7858, line 19, or at least it keeps us sharp to find the right page and the right line. But what I would like to invite to you to is -- if you look at what is said approximately these pages where we find, because that apparently was your argument, that the Chamber was willing to deviate from the text rather than to, as it seems to me at first sight, say, We're willing, we're prepared to hear some submissions if there is something really without evidence not primarily to decide, then, on anything smaller than a count but rather to encourage the Prosecution to withdraw a similar exercise is, of course, this Chamber has encouraged the Prosecution to do as well. So if you find anywhere where they clearly say, Well, even on the new text we feel free not to acquit on counts but even on portions of counts, then I'd like to know where it find that exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKHAVAN
utterances.text: If I may just briefly explain, Mr. President, we will produce, if you wish, the relevant citation for the entire portion of the oral decision under Rule 98 bis. My understanding is that the defendant in that case declined to request partial dismissal of counts but was invited to do so by the Trial Chamber. But I will confirm that and produce the relevant portions of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can just address that point briefly. It's my understanding of what happened in the Oric case that the Trial Chamber subsequent to 98 bis hearing then issued an order to the Defence in the Defence case that it need not address certain subjects. The defendant then appealed it, and I think Mr. Akhavan -- well, what we are saying in terms of the relief that we seek is we're -- ultimately the bottom line is if there's a matter that need not be addressed, even if it's partial to a count, there is no point in terms of efficiency that we then mount a defence on an account -- or portions of it that the Chamber feels no need to address. The Oric Trial Chamber issued an order telling the Defence don't address the following topics. The Defence appealed it, but what we're asking for here is that if in fact the Chamber wishes to invite the Defence in the Defence case, should there be a Defence case, that it need not address certain matters, we would certainly invite such an approach from the Chamber as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is a different -- I would say procedurally a different approach, and -- now the matter becomes clearer to me. Mr. Tieger, tomorrow, first session, one hour and a half still for the Prosecution to go. We will adjourn and resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 25th of March, 9.00 in the morning at Courtroom I.
